nameStory: The flexed gyro gets its name from its shell's distinctive twisted or 'flexed' appearance, combined with its spinning, gyroscope-like movement as it glides through the water. The word 'gyro' comes from the Greek word for circle or spiral, perfectly describing how these tiny snails navigate their aquatic world.
description: The flexed gyro is a tiny freshwater snail that lives in ponds, streams, and other quiet waters throughout North America. Its shell is flat and coiled like a miniature spiral, typically measuring just a few millimeters across - small enough to sit comfortably on your fingernail. These little aquatic wanderers belong to the ramshorn snail family, though they're much smaller than their more familiar cousins. You'll need to look closely to spot these delicate creatures as they glide along underwater surfaces.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Flat, disc-like spiral shell that coils in one plane, resembling a tiny cinnamon roll when viewed from above

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, typically 2-4 millimeters across - about the size of a small peppercorn

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth, translucent shell that feels delicate and paper-thin if gently touched

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale brown to amber shell that's often nearly transparent, allowing you to see the snail's body inside

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along underwater surfaces and plants with a characteristic rotating motion

habitat: Flexed gyros live in quiet freshwater environments throughout New England, including shallow ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and the calm edges of larger lakes. They prefer areas with aquatic vegetation where they can graze on algae and organic matter. Look for them on submerged plants, rocks, or crawling along muddy bottoms in areas with little to no current.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found grazing on early algae growth on rocks and emerging aquatic plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot moving along submerged vegetation and pond surfaces during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as temperatures drop, often found deeper in the water column.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant in northern areas, buried in sediment or hiding among plant debris under ice.

funFact: Despite being tiny enough to fit through the eye of a needle, flexed gyros are actually important ecosystem engineers - they help keep aquatic environments healthy by constantly scraping algae and bacteria from surfaces, acting like miniature underwater vacuum cleaners that work 24/7!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other tiny ramshorn snails, but the flexed gyro's extremely small size and delicate, nearly flat shell help distinguish it. Remember: if it looks like a microscopic nautilus shell and you need to squint to see it clearly, you've probably found a flexed gyro.
contextualKnowledge: This is an extremely rare find in New England with only one recorded observation, making any sighting scientifically valuable. The name 'ramshorn' refers to the curved horn of a male sheep (ram), describing the spiral shape these snails share, though flexed gyros are much more tightly coiled than typical ramshorns.
compareHints: Compared to its relative the disc gyro, the flexed gyro is smaller and has a more tightly wound, flatter spiral shell. While disc gyros have more obvious growth rings and a slightly more inflated appearance, flexed gyros look almost paper-thin from the side. Both are much smaller than the common ramshorn snails most people know.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The disc gyro can be distinguished from its relative, the flexed gyro, by its more consistently flat profile and tighter coiling pattern.
